description:
Four payments. Zero interest. Nothing extra to pay. So who is paying for it?

Klarna does not lend you money — it pays the shop in full, today, and then you owe Klarna. That one fact decides everything that follows.

The shop does not receive the full price. On a £90 jacket it receives around £85; the rest is the merchant fee, often about 3-6%. No shop absorbs that. It goes into the sticker — which means the price rises for everyone in that shop, including the person paying cash who has never used the app.

Three questions that settle it, whatever the brand:

1. Is this a sale, or a loan? They paid the shop; you owe them. That is a loan.
2. Does anyone profit from that loan? Not from you — from the merchant's fee. A loan that brings a benefit to the lender is the exact phrase scholars argue over.
3. Would cash have been cheaper? If later costs more than now, you paid for time.

Scholars genuinely differ. Same price as cash, no late fee, no interest — and many permit it. Add a penalty that becomes the lender's profit, or a higher price for paying later, and the disagreement ends.

And "buy now, pay later" was never the problem. Islam has had it for fourteen hundred years — murabaha. The seller buys the thing, actually owns it, and sells it to you at one disclosed price, fixed at signing, paid over time. Late? You owe the same. Not a penny more.

One price. One owner. No penalty.

The problem was never "pay later". It is who earns on the "later".

No jargon. Just mechanisms.
This is financial education, not financial advice. BNPL terms, merchant fees and late-fee policies differ by country and change often — check your own provider's current terms before you use them. Figures on screen are worked from a £90 basket to show the mechanism, not quoted from any provider's rate card.
